summary: Iceland is one of the 29 Schengen states: EEA/EFTA citizens enter with a valid passport or accepted identity card, visa-exempt nationalities get 90 days in any 180-day period (ETIAS is not yet in operation), and everyone else needs a €90 Schengen short-stay visa. Icelandic embassies issue visas in four cities; in about 120 other cities other Schengen states issue them on Iceland's behalf.

defaultSource.name: Regulation (EU) 2018/1806 listing visa-required and visa-exempt nationalities, consolidated text — EUR-Lex

defaultStayWindow.text: 90 days in any rolling 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area rather than per country. The day you arrive counts as the first day and the day you leave counts as the last. Leaving and coming back does not reset the allowance: on any given day, days already spent anywhere in the area during the preceding 180 still count against the 90.

fee.notes: €90 (children 6–11: €45; under 6: free). Icelandic embassies issue visas in four cities; in about 120 other cities other Schengen states issue visas on Iceland's behalf.

fee.notes: First residence permits cost ISK 40,000 to ISK 120,000 depending on the permit: ISK 80,000 for work, ISK 70,000 for students, ISK 110,000 for a spouse, ISK 60,000 for children, ISK 120,000 for au pairs and ISK 40,000 for working holiday. Iceland handles stays over 90 days (work, study, family) through residence permits issued by the Directorate of Immigration rather than long-stay visas.

passportValidity.text: Non-EU passports must be valid for at least 3 months beyond your planned departure from the Schengen Area and have been issued within the last 10 years.

proofOfFunds.text: Visitors must be able to show sufficient funds for their stay. Iceland's reference amount is ISK 8,000 per person per day, plus ISK 40,000 for each entry.

declarations.text: Non-EU travelers are registered biometrically (fingerprints and photo) in the EU Entry/Exit System at Schengen external borders. Registration happens at the border; there is nothing to submit in advance.

fee.notes: Free for under-18s and over-70s. Valid 3 years or until passport expiry.

declarations.text: Visa-exempt travelers will need an ETIAS travel authorization to enter the Schengen Area. It is not yet in operation, and no applications are being collected; the EU says it will announce the start date several months before launch.

currencyLimits.text: Cash of more than €10,000 (or the equivalent in other currencies, traveler's checks or bearer negotiable instruments) must be declared to customs when entering or leaving Iceland.

source.name: Skatturinn (Iceland Revenue and Customs) — Cash declaration

notes: Iceland Revenue and Customs says visitors may bring in duty-free up to 10 kg of food worth no more than ISK 25,000, but no meat or dairy products from outside the European Economic Area.

The duty-free alcohol allowance is a set of combinations, for example 1 litre of spirits, 0.75 litre of wine and 3 litres of beer, or 18 litres of beer; the tobacco allowance is 200 cigarettes or 250 g of other tobacco. You must be 20 to bring in alcohol and 18 for tobacco.

Angling gear and riding clothing used abroad must be disinfected, with a certificate from an authorised veterinary officer or at your own cost on arrival; used leather riding gear such as saddles and bridles may not be imported.

safety.text: The UK FCDO says crime levels are low but petty theft and antisocial behaviour can occur, particularly around bars in downtown Reykjavík; that weather can change quickly and strong winds can damage rental cars; and that there have been a series of volcanic eruptions on the Reykjanes peninsula since December 2023, so follow the authorities' advice.

bestTimeToVisit.text: No official source we could read gives a best time to visit Iceland. Canada's travel advice says roads in the highlands and other remote areas are open only in summer, and that winter tires are mandatory between November and April.

idp.text: Iceland is a party to the 1949 Geneva Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1968 Vienna one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1949 Geneva version. A permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention carries no treaty obligation here.

tips.text: The UK Foreign Office says the weather can change quickly and make driving challenging, that some highland and interior roads require four-wheel drive, and that river levels can change within the same day. Check road and weather information from the Icelandic Road and Coastal Administration and Safe Travel Iceland before setting out.

The UK Foreign Office says strong winds can throw up sand or ash and damage paintwork, that such weather damage to rental cars may not be covered by insurance, and that British tourists have had to pay large repair bills.
Iceland applies EU border systems: non-EU visitors are registered in the Entry/Exit System at the border, and the ETIAS travel authorization for visa-exempt travelers is not yet in operation.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Iceland?
faq.answer: EEA/EFTA citizens enter with a valid passport or accepted identity card. Citizens of the countries on the EU's visa-free list — including the US, UK, Canada, Australia and Japan — can visit visa-free for 90 days in any 180-day period. Everyone else needs a Schengen short-stay visa (€90); in about 120 cities other Schengen states issue visas on Iceland's behalf.

faq.question: Is Iceland in the Schengen Area even though it is not in the EU?
faq.answer: Yes. Iceland's Directorate of Immigration lists Iceland among the 29 Schengen states; a Schengen visa issued by any of them is valid for Iceland, and the 90-days-in-180 allowance covers the whole Schengen area.

faq.question: Do I need ETIAS to visit Iceland?
faq.answer: Once ETIAS becomes mandatory, visa-exempt non-EU travelers will need the €20 online authorization before traveling to Iceland and the rest of the Schengen Area. It is not yet in operation, and no applications are being collected; the EU says it will announce the start date several months before launch.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for an Icelandair or PLAY stopover in Iceland?
faq.answer: Iceland's Directorate of Immigration says a traveller flying from outside Schengen to Iceland and on to another Schengen airport is entering the Schengen area in Iceland and needs a Schengen visa if their nationality requires one. Only a journey from a non-Schengen country through Iceland to another non-Schengen country counts as transit, for which some nationalities need an Airport Transit Visa.

faq.question: Is it safe to drive in Iceland in winter?
faq.answer: Canada's travel advice says driving can be hazardous, particularly in winter; winter tires are mandatory between November and April, and highland and other remote roads are open only in summer. Check road conditions with the Icelandic Road and Coastal Administration and Safe Travel Iceland before you set out.
